stem: A company issues employee IDs made of one department letter from $\{A,B,C,D,E\}$ followed by a four-digit number. The first digit of the number may not be 0 and the last digit must be odd; the middle two digits are unrestricted. How many different IDs can be issued?

options.why: This ignores both restrictions on the number: the first digit cannot be 0 and the last must be odd.
The restriction on the last digit (odd) has not been applied.
There are 5 odd digits (1, 3, 5, 7, 9), not 4.

solution: Fill the positions one at a time and multiply the number of choices.
Letter: 5. First digit: 9 (1 to 9). Two middle digits: 10 each. Last digit: 5 (odd).
hints: Choose each character in turn and ask how many options remain for that position.
The first digit has 9 options, the last has 5; they can be chosen independently of the others.
Multiply: 5 letters, 9, 10, 10, 5.
misconception: Applying a restriction to the wrong position or forgetting one.
why: The number of codes is the product of the choices at each independent position.

stem: Four panellists and a moderator are to sit in a row of five chairs for a broadcast. The moderator must take one of the two end chairs. In how many different ways can the five people be seated?

options.why: This ignores the restriction on the moderator and counts all arrangements of five people.
The moderator can take either end chair; this counts only one of them.
After placing the moderator, all four panellists can be arranged in the remaining chairs: $4!$, not $3!$.

solution: The moderator has 2 possible chairs. The four panellists then fill the remaining four chairs in $4! = 24$ ways.
hints: Place the person with the restriction first.
How many choices does the moderator have, and then how many people remain to arrange?
Multiply the two stages.
concept: Counting permutations after fixing a restricted object.
misconception: Using $5!$ and forgetting the restriction.
why: The moderator’s choice and the panellists’ order are independent stages.

stem: Six distinct books are placed on a shelf: 3 statistics books, 2 econometrics books and 1 dictionary. The three statistics books must stand together and the two econometrics books must stand together. How many arrangements are possible?

options.why: This arranges the statistics books among themselves and the econometrics books among themselves but never orders the three blocks.
This ignores the requirement that each subject’s books stand together.
The order within the two-book block is already included once as $2!$; doubling counts it again.

solution: Treat the statistics books as one block and the econometrics books as another. With the dictionary there are 3 units, arranged in $3! = 6$ ways.
Within the statistics block the books can be ordered in $3! = 6$ ways, within the econometrics block in $2! = 2$ ways.
hints: Think of each group that must stay together as a single object first.
How many objects are there on the shelf once the blocks are formed, and in how many orders?
Then multiply by the number of orderings inside each block.
misconception: Forgetting to order the blocks themselves.
why: Block order and within-block order are independent choices, so their counts multiply.

stem: Three couples are to be seated at a round table with six identical chairs. Two seatings are the same if one is a rotation of the other. In how many distinct ways can they be seated if each couple must sit side by side?

options.why: Three blocks around a circle can be arranged in $(3-1)! = 2$ ways, not $3!$; rotations are the same seating.
This orders the couples around the table but ignores the two possible orders within each couple.
This is the number of circular arrangements of six people with no couple restriction.

solution: Treat each couple as a block: 3 blocks around a circle can be arranged in $(3-1)! = 2$ ways, since rotations are identical.
Within each block the two partners can swap places: $2^3 = 8$ ways.
hints: Combine each couple into one object; how many objects sit around the table?
For $n$ objects around a circle, rotations are equivalent: there are $(n-1)!$ arrangements.
Each couple can be seated in 2 internal orders.
misconception: Using $n!$ for a circle without removing rotations.
why: Fixing one block removes the rotational symmetry, leaving $(n-1)!$ patterns.

stem: A student lists every distinct way of re-ordering all nine letters of the word ECONOMICS, never writing the same string twice. How many entries will the list contain?

options.why: This treats the two C’s and the two O’s as distinguishable letters.
Only one repeated letter has been divided out; both C and O occur twice.
A third repeated letter has been assumed; only C and O repeat (E, N, M, I, S occur once).

solution: ECONOMICS has 9 letters: C occurs twice, O occurs twice, and E, N, M, I, S once each.
If all letters were different there would be $9!$ arrangements; swapping the two C’s or the two O’s gives the same word, so divide by $2!\,2!$.
hints: Count how many times each letter appears in the word.
Start from $9!$ and correct for indistinguishable repeats.
Divide by $2!$ for each letter that occurs twice.
misconception: Using $n!$ when some objects are identical.
why: Each distinct word is counted $2!\,2!$ times among the $9!$ labelled arrangements.

stem: A fund manager must choose 3 stocks for a portfolio from a watch-list of 12 stocks, of which 4 are technology stocks. How many portfolios contain at least one technology stock?

options.why: This counts only portfolios with exactly one technology stock; portfolios with two or three also qualify.
This is the number of portfolios with no technology stock.
This counts all portfolios, including those with no technology stock.

solution: Portfolios with no technology stock use only the 8 others: $\binom{8}{3} = 56$.
hints: "At least one" is usually easier through its opposite.
How many portfolios contain no technology stock at all?
Subtract that count from the total number of portfolios.
concept: Counting "at least one" with the complement.
misconception: Choosing one special item and then anything, which double counts.
why: Every portfolio either has no technology stock or at least one, never both.

stem: A department of 10 faculty members forms a 3-person hiring panel and then names one of the three as chair. In how many ways can the panel and its chair be chosen?

options.why: This counts only the panels; each panel can be given a chair in three ways.
This treats the three roles as all different (ordered selection), but only the chair is special.
The chair must be one of the three panel members, not any of the ten faculty members.

solution: Choose the panel: $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ ways. Choose the chair from the three: 3 ways.
Check: choose the chair first (10 ways), then the other two members $\binom{9}{2} = 36$: $10\times36 = 360$.
hints: Is the order of the panel members relevant? What distinguishes one member?
Choose the panel first, then the chair.
You can verify by choosing the chair first.
misconception: Using permutations for a set where only one member is special.
why: Two valid orders of choosing must produce the same total.

stem: A project team of 5 is to be chosen from 11 candidates, including individuals $A$, $B$, $P$ and $Q$. $A$ and $B$ will not serve on the same team, and the team must contain at least one of $P$ and $Q$. How many teams are possible?

options.why: Teams containing both $A$ and $B$ and neither of $P$, $Q$ have been subtracted twice; add them back once.
Only the restriction on $A$ and $B$ was applied; the team must also contain $P$ or $Q$.
This adds the two sets of unwanted teams instead of removing them from the total.

solution: Bad type 1: both $A$ and $B$ on the team: $\binom{9}{3} = 84$.
Bad type 2: neither $P$ nor $Q$: choose all 5 from the other 9: $\binom{9}{5} = 126$.
Both bad types: $A$, $B$ on, $P$, $Q$ off: choose 3 from the remaining 7: $\binom{7}{3} = 35$.
hints: Count the teams that break at least one rule and subtract from the total.
The two ways of breaking the rules can happen together, so use inclusion-exclusion.
In the overlap, $A$ and $B$ are on the team, $P$ and $Q$ are off, and 3 places are filled from 7 others.
concept: Inclusion-exclusion for selections with two simultaneous constraints.
misconception: Subtracting two overlapping bad sets without restoring their intersection.
why: A team that breaks both rules is removed twice by simple subtraction, so it must be added back once.

stem: A delivery robot moves on a city grid from the depot at $(0,0)$ to a customer at $(5,3)$, taking only unit steps east or north. It must pass through the charging point at $(2,1)$. How many different routes are there?

options.why: This counts all routes from $(0,0)$ to $(5,3)$, ignoring the required charging point.
The numbers of routes for the two legs must be multiplied, not added.
The second leg has 3 east and 2 north steps: $\binom{5}{2}$ routes; an extra factor of 2 has no basis.

solution: Leg 1: $(0,0)\to(2,1)$ needs 2 east and 1 north steps: $\binom{3}{1} = 3$ routes.
Leg 2: $(2,1)\to(5,3)$ needs 3 east and 2 north steps: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ routes.
hints: A route through a given point splits into two independent legs.
Each leg is an arrangement of east and north steps.
Count each leg with a binomial coefficient and multiply.
concept: Counting lattice paths with a mandatory waypoint.
misconception: Counting all paths and forgetting the waypoint, or adding leg counts.
why: Every valid route corresponds to one choice for each leg.

stem: Ten students are split into a group of 4 for a macroeconomics project and two groups of 3 that will both work on the same microeconomics project (so these two groups are not distinguished from each other). In how many ways can the split be made?

options.why: This treats the two groups of 3 as labelled; swapping them gives the same split, so divide by 2.
Dividing by $3!$ would be right for three identical groups; only the two groups of 3 are identical.
Multiplying by 2 goes the wrong way: identical groups reduce the number of distinct splits.

solution: Choose the group of 4: $\binom{10}{4} = 210$. Choose one group of 3 from the remaining 6: $\binom{6}{3} = 20$; the rest form the other group.
That gives $210\times20 = 4200$ ordered choices, but the two groups of 3 are interchangeable, so each split has been counted twice.
hints: First count as if every group were labelled.
Which groups are interchangeable? How many times is each split counted?
Divide by the number of ways of ordering the identical groups.
concept: Partitions into groups with some groups indistinguishable.
misconception: Treating identical groups as labelled.
why: Each unlabelled split corresponds to exactly 2 labelled splits.

stem: A six-question multiple-choice quiz has options A, B, C and D for every question. How many different answer keys contain exactly two A's, two B's, one C and one D?

options.why: This treats all six answers as distinguishable; the two A’s are interchangeable, as are the two B’s.
This counts all possible answer keys, not only those with the specified composition.
The division by $2!\,2!$ already accounts for the repeated letters; the extra factor has no basis.

solution: Choose which two questions get A: $\binom{6}{2}$; which two of the remaining four get B: $\binom{4}{2}$; which of the last two gets C: $\binom{2}{1}$; the final question is D.
hints: An answer key is a way of labelling six positions with letters.
Choose the positions for each letter in turn.
The result is a multinomial coefficient.
misconception: Not dividing out identical labels.
why: The multinomial counts distinct arrangements of a multiset.

stem: A ministry distributes 14 identical grants among 5 regions. Regions 1 and 2 must each receive at least one grant; the other three regions may receive none. How many distributions are possible?

options.why: This ignores the minimum of one grant for regions 1 and 2.
This is the count when every region needs at least one grant; regions 3 to 5 may receive none.
The number of bars is one less than the number of regions (4), so the second argument should be 4.

solution: Give one grant to each of regions 1 and 2 first. That leaves 12 grants to distribute among 5 regions with no restrictions.
hints: Remove the compulsory grants first; what is left to distribute?
After that there are no restrictions, so use stars and bars.
Non-negative solutions of a sum to $n$ in $k$ variables: $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$.
concept: Stars and bars with lower bounds.
misconception: Using the formula for positive integers when only some variables are bounded below.
why: Shifting variables by their minimums turns bounded counts into unrestricted ones.

stem: Three friends each independently pick one of 5 restaurants at random for lunch (every restaurant is equally likely for each friend). What is the probability that all three choose different restaurants?

options.why: This is $1 - 2/5$, a guess that ignores that the third friend must avoid two restaurants.
The sample space for independent choices has $5^3 = 125$ outcomes, not a count of ordered selections without repeats.
The choices are ordered (friend 1, 2, 3), so each set of three restaurants corresponds to $3! = 6$ outcomes.

solution: Favourable: friend 1 has 5 options, friend 2 has 4 (different from friend 1), friend 3 has 3: $5\times4\times3 = 60$.
hints: How many outcomes are there when each friend chooses independently?
Count outcomes in which no restaurant is repeated by choosing in order.
Divide the favourable count by $5^3$.
concept: Probability of no repeats in sampling with replacement.
misconception: Using the without-replacement count for the denominator.
why: The probability is the ratio of the count of repeat-free sequences to all sequences.

stem: Five parcels are sent, each independently and with equal probability, to one of three depots. What is the probability that every depot receives at least one parcel?

options.why: This counts the outcomes that leave at least one depot empty (with overlaps counted twice), the opposite of the event asked for.
The outcomes in which two depots are empty were subtracted twice; add the 3 such outcomes back.
Choosing which depot receives which parcel in a fixed pattern does not count all onto assignments.

solution: Let $E_i$ be "depot $i$ empty". $|E_i| = 2^5 = 32$, $|E_i\cap E_j| = 1$, and all three empty is impossible.
hints: Count the assignments in which some depot is empty, then take the complement.
Use inclusion-exclusion over the events "depot $i$ is empty".
If depots $i$ and $j$ are both empty, every parcel goes to the third depot.
misconception: Subtracting overlapping cases without correcting for their intersections.
why: Alternating inclusion and exclusion counts each assignment with an empty depot exactly once.

sub: inclusion of specific items in a sample
stem: An auditor draws a simple random sample of 15 invoices from a batch of 120. Two particular invoices, $X$ and $Y$, are of special interest. What is the probability that exactly one of $X$ and $Y$ is in the sample?

options.why: This is the probability that both invoices are selected.
This adds the two inclusion probabilities and counts the case where both are selected twice.
The second factor should use the 119 invoices remaining after $X$ is considered, not the original 120.

solution: $P(X\text{ in}) = 15/120$. Given that, $Y$ is out with probability $\dfrac{105}{119}$ (105 of the 119 other invoices are not selected).
The same holds with $X$ and $Y$ exchanged, and the two cases are disjoint:
hints: Split the event into two disjoint cases according to which invoice is selected.
Given $X$ is in the sample, what is the chance that $Y$ is not?
A random sample is symmetric between invoices, so the two cases have equal probability.
concept: Inclusion probabilities in simple random sampling.
misconception: Using the unconditional probability for the second invoice.
why: Sampling without replacement makes the second inclusion probability depend on the first.

stem: Four players are each dealt 13 cards from a freshly shuffled pack. What is the probability that every player ends up holding exactly one of the four kings?

options.why: This treats the four kings as if each were assigned to a player with independent equal chances, which is the right count only for the first king.
The kings can go to the four players in $4! = 24$ ways; this counts only one assignment.
This uses independent draws with replacement; the kings occupy distinct cards, so the denominator is $52\cdot51\cdot50\cdot49$.

solution: Think of the positions of the four kings among the 52 dealt positions. Each position belongs to a player (13 positions each).
Favourable ordered placements of the 4 distinct kings: choose a player for each king so all differ ($4!$), and a position in that player’s 13: $4!\cdot13^4$.
hints: Place the four kings one at a time into the 52 positions.
For a favourable outcome the kings go to four different players: how many assignments of kings to players are there?
Each king then has 13 positions in its player’s hand; the total number of ordered placements is $52\cdot51\cdot50\cdot49$.
concept: Counting equally likely placements of distinguished cards.
misconception: Using independent probabilities for sampling without replacement.
why: All ordered placements of the kings are equally likely, so probability is a ratio of counts.

stem: The eleven letters of MISSISSIPPI are arranged in a random order. What is the probability that the four S's appear consecutively?

options.why: After gluing the S’s there are 8 objects (the block, M, four I’s, two P’s) to arrange, not 7.
A run of four adjacent slots among 11 can start at slots 1 to 8, so there are 8 favourable slot sets, not 9.
There is no reason for the probability to equal a single-letter proportion.

solution: Glue the four S’s into one block. The objects are the block, M, four I’s and two P’s: $\dfrac{8!}{4!\,2!} = 840$ arrangements.
hints: Count the distinct arrangements of all letters first.
For the favourable count, treat the four S’s as a single block.
The block, M, four I’s and two P’s are the objects to arrange.
concept: Probability that identical objects are adjacent.
misconception: Miscounting the objects after forming a block.
why: Both counts use the same notion of "distinct arrangement", so their ratio is the probability.

stem: How many six-digit numbers (no leading zero) have no repeated digit and are divisible by 5?

options.why: When the last digit is 5 the first digit has only 8 options (not 0 and not 5), so the two cases have different counts.
This counts only numbers ending in 0; numbers ending in 5 also qualify.
The last digit is fixed first (0 or 5); the other digits then lose options one at a time.

solution: A number divisible by 5 ends in 0 or 5.
Ends in 0: the other five digits are an ordered selection from 1 to 9: $9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5 = 15\,120$.
Ends in 5: first digit from $\{1,\dots,9\}\setminus\{5\}$: 8; then four more digits from the 8 remaining (0 is now allowed): $8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5 = 1680$. Total $8\times1680 = 13\,440$.
hints: Split by the last digit, since it determines divisibility.
When the last digit is 0, there is no further restriction on the leading digit; when it is 5, 0 is no longer excluded from the middle but the first digit still cannot be 0.
Fill the leading digit first in the second case.
concept: Cases with restrictions on first and last digits.
misconception: Assuming the two cases have the same count.
why: The leading-digit restriction interacts with the choice of last digit.

stem: A consultancy has 7 analysts available and 4 different tasks to allocate, one analyst per task, no analyst taking more than one task. In how many ways can the tasks be allocated?

options.why: This ignores which task each analyst does; the tasks are different, so order matters.
This allows the same analyst to take several tasks.
This arranges all seven analysts; only four tasks are assigned.

solution: The first task can go to any of 7 analysts, the second to any of the remaining 6, then 5, then 4.
hints: Are the tasks interchangeable or different from each other?
Assign the tasks in sequence; how many analysts remain each time?
This is a permutation of 4 chosen from 7.
misconception: Using combinations when positions are distinguishable.
why: Different tasks make each assignment an ordered selection.

stem: A committee of 5 is chosen at random from 7 first-year, 6 second-year and 5 third-year students. What is the probability that exactly two of the three year groups are represented on the committee?

options.why: These counts include committees drawn entirely from one year, which represent only one group.
This is the probability that at least two groups are represented, including committees with all three.
Only one pair of year groups was considered; any of the three pairs can be the represented pair.

solution: For a given pair of year groups, committees using only those two groups but not just one of them: $\binom{a+b}{5} - \binom{a}{5} - \binom{b}{5}$.
hints: Fix which two year groups are represented and count the committees using exactly those two.
Within a pair, subtract the committees that come entirely from one of the two years.
Add the three pair counts and divide by $\binom{18}{5}$.
concept: Counting committees with exactly $k$ of several groups represented.
misconception: Including single-group committees in each pair count.
why: Each committee with exactly two represented groups belongs to exactly one pair.

stem: Twelve research proposals, 4 of them on infrastructure, are presented to a panel in a uniformly random order. What is the probability that the four infrastructure proposals are presented consecutively (in some order, in four adjacent slots)?

options.why: This is the probability that all four fall in the first six slots, a different event.
A block of four slots can start at positions 1 to 9 only, so there are 9 starting points, not 12.
The probability depends on the number of ways the four slots can be placed among all $\binom{12}{4}$ sets of slots.

solution: The set of slots occupied by the infrastructure proposals is equally likely to be any of $\binom{12}{4} = 495$ four-element subsets.
The subset is four consecutive slots if it starts at slot 1, 2, …, 9: 9 subsets.
hints: Only the set of occupied slots matters; all sets of four slots are equally likely.
How many sets of four slots are consecutive?
A run of four starting at slot $s$ needs $s+3\le12$.
concept: Random placement of special items among positions.
misconception: Counting starting points incorrectly or ignoring the equal-likelihood of slot sets.
why: By symmetry the occupied slots are a uniformly random 4-subset.

stem: Five cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability of being dealt exactly three of a kind: three cards of one rank and two other cards of two different ranks (so a full house or four of a kind does not count)?

options.why: Choosing any two other cards can produce a full house or four of a kind, which must be excluded.
The suits of the two other cards must also be chosen: $4\times4$ ways.
Three cards of different ranks are not three of a kind; the three equal-rank cards come from one rank.

solution: Rank of the triple: 13. Choose 3 of its 4 suits: $\binom43 = 4$.
Two other ranks (different from each other and from the triple): $\binom{12}{2} = 66$; a suit for each: $4\cdot4 = 16$.
hints: Build the hand in stages: the rank of the triple, then its suits.
The other two cards must have different ranks, both different from the triple.
Don’t forget to choose the suit for each of the two other cards.
concept: Classical probability with a structured count.
misconception: Allowing the two extra cards to match each other or the triple.
why: Each hand of this type is generated exactly once by the staged construction.

stem: A three-character access code uses the letters A, B, C, D, E, with repetition allowed. How many codes contain at least one repeated letter?

options.why: This is the number of codes with no repeated letter.
This counts all codes, not only those with a repeat.
This subtracts only the 5 codes in which all three letters are equal, as if "no repeat" meant "all letters the same". Codes with different letters number $5\cdot4\cdot3 = 60$.

hints: Count the opposite event: all letters different.
How many codes are there in total when repetition is allowed?
Subtract the no-repeat count from the total number of codes.
misconception: Trying to count each repeat pattern separately and missing some.
why: The events "some repeat" and "no repeat" partition the codes.

sub: solving for an unknown population size
stem: A bag contains red and blue balls, with 4 more blue balls than red balls and fewer than 50 balls in total. Two balls are drawn without replacement. The probability that they have the same colour is $47/95$. How many balls are in the bag?

options.why: This is the larger root of the quadratic ($r=36$ red, 40 blue), which is excluded by "fewer than 50 balls".
This is the number of red balls $r$, not the total.
This does not satisfy the equation; check $P(\text{same})$ for $r=10$.

solution: Let there be $r$ red and $r+4$ blue balls: $n = 2r+4$.
$r = 36$ gives 76 balls, which violates "fewer than 50", so $r=8$, 12 blue, $n = 20$.
hints: Express the probability in terms of the number of red balls $r$.
Set it equal to $47/95$ and rearrange to a quadratic in $r$.
Two roots appear; which one satisfies the size condition?
concept: Using a probability equation to recover a population size.
misconception: Accepting both roots of the quadratic or reporting a component instead of the total.
why: The quadratic arises because the same-colour probability is a ratio of quadratics in $r$.

stem: Five analysts $A, B, C, D, E$ line up for a photograph. In how many orders are $A$ and $B$ not standing next to each other?

options.why: This is the number of orders in which $A$ and $B$ are adjacent.
Adjacent pairs can occur as $AB$ or $BA$; the block can be ordered in 2 ways.
This ignores the restriction.

solution: Orders with $A$ and $B$ adjacent: treat them as a block ($4!$ orders of 4 units) and order the block internally in 2 ways: $2\cdot24 = 48$.
hints: Count the complement: orders in which they are adjacent.
Glue $A$ and $B$ into one unit; in how many ways can the pair itself be ordered?
Subtract from $5!$.
misconception: Forgetting the internal order of the block.
why: Restrictions "not together" are usually easiest through the complement.

stem: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of the word BUDGET can be made in which the two vowels, U and E, are next to each other?

options.why: The vowel block can be written as UE or EU, doubling the count.
This ignores the requirement that the vowels be adjacent.
After forming the block there are 5 units (the block and 4 consonants), so $5!$ orders, not $4!$.

solution: Form a block from U and E: 2 internal orders.
The block and the four consonants B, D, G, T give 5 units: $5! = 120$ orders.
hints: Treat the two vowels as a single unit.
How many units are there, and in how many orders?
Multiply by the internal orderings of the block.
misconception: Counting the block as a single arrangement.
why: Block order and internal order are independent choices.

stem: At a networking event each of 12 attendees shakes hands exactly once with every other attendee. How many handshakes take place?
solution: Each handshake is an unordered pair of attendees: $\binom{12}{2} = \dfrac{12\cdot11}{2} = 66$.
hints: Is a handshake between $a$ and $b$ different from one between $b$ and $a$?
Count pairs, not ordered pairs.
Compute $\binom{12}{2}$.
misconception: Using $12\times11$ without dividing by 2.
why: Each pair is counted twice among ordered pairs.

sub: selection with at least from each group
stem: A panel of 4 is to be chosen from 5 economists and 4 sociologists, and must contain at least one person from each discipline. How many panels are possible?

options.why: This includes panels made up of only economists or only sociologists.
The all-sociologist panel is also excluded: it contains no economist.
Choosing one of each first and then any two others counts panels with several members of a discipline more than once.

hints: Which panels violate the requirement?
There are two kinds of bad panel; neither overlaps the other.
Subtract both from the total.
concept: Counting with a requirement of representation.
misconception: Over-counting by choosing the required members first.
why: The complement consists of two disjoint, small cases.

stem: A binary access code has 8 bits. How many codes contain no two consecutive 1s?
solution: Let $a_n$ count valid strings of length $n$. A valid string ends in 0 (any valid string of length $n-1$ before it) or in 01 (any valid string of length $n-2$ before that).
hints: Look at the last bit of a valid string.
If the last bit is 1, what must the bit before it be?
Build the sequence $a_n = a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ up to $n=8$.
misconception: Trying to count by inclusion-exclusion without a pattern.
why: Each valid string is built uniquely from a shorter valid string.

stem: A 4-character PIN uses digits 0 to 9 with repetition allowed. How many PINs contain at least one 7?

options.why: Choosing the position of a 7 and then anything counts PINs with several 7s more than once.
This is the number of PINs with no 7.
There are four positions, so the number without a 7 is $9^4$, not $9^3$.

hints: Count the PINs that contain no 7 at all.
Each position then has 9 options.
Subtract from the total number of PINs.
misconception: Choosing the special digit first and over-counting.
why: The complement is a single product.

stem: A fund manager is considering 7 candidate stocks and may include any subset in a portfolio, including holding none. How many different portfolios (subsets) are possible?
solution: Each stock is either in or out: $2^7 = 128$ portfolios (including the empty portfolio).
hints: For each stock there are two possibilities.
The decisions are independent.
Multiply seven 2’s.
misconception: Counting only portfolios of a fixed size.
why: A subset corresponds to a sequence of in/out decisions.

stem: A cafe sells 5 kinds of pastry. In how many ways can a customer choose a box of 8 pastries if the order does not matter and each kind may be chosen any number of times?

options.why: This chooses 5 of 8 distinct items; here 8 pastries are taken from 5 kinds, with repetition allowed.
This counts ordered selections, but the order of pastries in the box does not matter.
The number of bars is one less than the number of kinds: $\binom{8+4}{4}$, not $\binom{8+5}{5}$.

solution: The number of multisets of size 8 from 5 kinds equals the number of non-negative integer solutions of $x_1+\dots+x_5 = 8$.
hints: Only how many of each kind matters, not the order.
Translate to counting non-negative integer solutions of a sum.
Use $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$.
misconception: Using ordered counts or the wrong bar count.
why: A selection is a list of five counts adding to 8.

stem: In a round-robin tournament each of 9 teams plays every other team exactly twice (home and away). How many matches are played in total?
solution: Pairs of teams: $\binom92 = 36$. Each pair meets twice: $72$ matches.
Equivalently each team plays $8\times2$ matches, and each match involves two teams: $9\cdot16/2 = 72$.
hints: How many different pairs of teams are there?
Each pair plays more than once.
Multiply by the number of meetings.
misconception: Counting each match twice.
why: Home and away matches are different events for the same pair.

stem: A lottery draws 6 distinct numbers from 1 to 40. A ticket has 6 distinct numbers. What is the probability that a ticket matches all six drawn numbers? Give the answer as a decimal to 8 places, e.g. 0.00000026.
solution: The number of possible draws is $\binom{40}{6} = 3\,838\,380$, all equally likely.
One of them matches the ticket: $P = 1/3\,838\,380 \approx 2.6\times10^{-7}$.
hints: The order in which numbers are drawn does not matter.
How many different sets of 6 numbers can be drawn from 40?
Only one set matches the ticket.
misconception: Using ordered selections ($40\cdot39\cdots$) in the denominator.
why: Each 6-subset is equally likely to be drawn.

stem: A committee of 4 is chosen from 10 people numbered 1 to 10. Classifying each committee by its lowest-numbered member $k$ shows that the number of committees equals $\sum_{k=1}^{7}\binom{10-k}{3}$. What is the value of this sum?

options.why: The sum counts committees of 4, so it equals $\binom{10}{4}$, not $\binom{10}{3}$.
The hockey-stick sum stops at $\binom{9}{3}$ for $k=1$, giving $\binom{10}{4}$, not $\binom{11}{4}$.
The terms decrease with $k$; they are not all equal to $\binom93$.

solution: Every committee of 4 has a unique lowest-numbered member $k$; the other 3 members are chosen from the $10-k$ people above $k$: $\binom{10-k}{3}$ committees.
Summing over $k$ counts every committee once, so the sum is $\binom{10}{4} = 210$.
hints: Classify each committee by its smallest member.
If the smallest member is $k$, how many choices remain for the other three?
Every committee has exactly one smallest member.
concept: Counting the same set in two ways.
misconception: Evaluating the sum numerically with an arithmetic slip.
why: The sum and $\binom{10}{4}$ count the same collection of committees.

stem: Six different invoices are each assigned to one of 3 approvers (an approver may receive any number, including none). How many assignments are possible?

options.why: This would assign 3 invoices to 6 approvers; here each of the 6 invoices chooses one of 3 approvers.
This counts distributions of identical items; the invoices are different.
Approvers can receive several invoices, so this restricted count is not appropriate.

solution: Each invoice independently chooses one of 3 approvers: $3^6 = 729$ assignments.
hints: Does an approver have to receive at most one invoice?
Each invoice has its own independent choice.
Multiply the choices.
concept: Assignments of distinguishable objects to labelled boxes.
misconception: Mixing up which set is the domain.
why: Each assignment is a function from invoices to approvers.

stem: Four employees each write their name on a gift tag and the four gifts are shuffled and handed out one per employee. In how many of the $4!$ distributions does nobody receive their own gift?

options.why: This is $24-9$: the number of distributions in which at least one employee receives their own gift.
This is the number of distributions with exactly two correct gifts.
This counts only the distributions made of two swapped pairs; four-cycles also leave nobody with their own gift.

solution: Inclusion-exclusion over "employee $i$ gets their own gift":
hints: Count the complement: distributions with at least one fixed point.
If $k$ specific employees get their own gifts, the rest can be arranged in $(4-k)!$ ways.
Alternate signs: $24-24+12-4+1$.
misconception: Subtracting only the single-match cases.
why: Each distribution with several matches is counted by the alternating sum exactly once.

stem: Seven applicants are ranked into three outcome bands: 2 receive "strong", 3 receive "adequate" and 2 receive "weak". In how many different ways can the bands be allocated to the 7 distinct applicants?

options.why: This treats the labels as all different; applicants in the same band are interchangeable in label.
After choosing the strong and adequate groups the weak group is determined, so there is no further factor of 2.
This counts all assignments of three labels, not only those with the specified numbers.

solution: Choose which 2 applicants are "strong": $\binom72 = 21$. From the remaining 5 choose 3 for "adequate": $\binom53 = 10$. The last 2 are "weak".
hints: Choose the members of each band in turn.
After two bands are filled, the third is forced.
This is a multinomial coefficient.
misconception: Using $7!$ or $3^7$.
why: The multinomial counts labellings with prescribed numbers per label.

stem: A company has 400 employees. Which statement can be guaranteed to be true?

answer.display: At least two employees share a birthday (day of the year)

options.text: At least two employees share a birthday (day of the year)
At least 10 employees share a birthday
options.why: Spread evenly, about 1.1 per day: at least 2 per day is guaranteed, but not 10.

options.text: At least one birthday is shared by exactly two employees
options.why: Some days could have 3 or more employees and none exactly two; the guarantee is only that some day has at least two.

options.text: Every day of the year is the birthday of at least one employee
options.why: With 400 employees it is possible that some days are missed.

solution: There are at most 366 possible birthdays and 400 employees.
By the pigeonhole principle at least $\lceil400/366\rceil = 2$ employees share a day.
hints: How many "boxes" (birthdays) are there?
If everyone had a different birthday, how many employees could there be at most?
Which statement follows with certainty, not just likelihood?
misconception: Confusing "likely" with "guaranteed".
why: More objects than boxes forces a box with at least two.

stem: A working group of 5 is chosen from 12 staff. The head of department must be in the group and two particular rivals, $R_1$ and $R_2$, must not both be chosen. How many groups are possible? (The head is neither $R_1$ nor $R_2$.)

options.why: This ignores the restriction on the two rivals.
Fixing both rivals leaves 9 people (excluding the head and the rivals) for 2 more places: $\binom92$.
The head of department must be in the group, so the base count is $\binom{11}{4}$.

solution: With the head fixed, choose 4 more from the other 11: $\binom{11}{4} = 330$.
Groups containing both rivals: choose 2 more from the remaining 9: $\binom92 = 36$.
hints: Fix the head first; how many places and people remain?
Count the groups that contain both rivals.
Subtract the groups containing both rivals from the total.
concept: Counting with a required member and a forbidden pair.
misconception: Forgetting to fix the head.
why: Fixing members reduces the problem to a smaller selection.

sub: ways to reach a total with dice
stem: Three fair dice are rolled. In how many of the 216 ordered outcomes is the sum equal to 10?
solution: Distinct values give $3! = 6$ orders; two equal values give 3 orders.
hints: List the unordered triples of values from 1 to 6 that sum to 10.
For each, count the number of distinct orderings.
Triples with a repeated value have 3 orderings, with three distinct values 6.
concept: Counting ordered outcomes with a fixed sum.
misconception: Counting only unordered triples.
why: Each unordered triple corresponds to a number of ordered outcomes by its multiplicity pattern.

stem: Seven directors sit at a round table (rotations count as the same seating). Two of them, $P$ and $Q$, refuse to sit next to each other. How many seatings are possible?

options.why: This is the number of seatings in which $P$ and $Q$ are adjacent.
These are linear-order counts; around a circular table fix one person to remove rotations: $6!$ in total.
The adjacent pair can sit as $PQ$ or $QP$, so $2\cdot5!$ must be removed.

solution: $P,Q$ adjacent: treat them as a block; 6 units around a circle: $5! = 120$, times 2 internal orders $=240$.
hints: How many circular arrangements of 7 people are there?
Count the arrangements in which $P$ and $Q$ sit together.
Subtract the adjacent seatings from all circular seatings.
concept: Circular permutations with an adjacency restriction.
misconception: Using linear counts or forgetting the internal order of the block.
why: Rotational symmetry is removed by fixing one person.

stem: A courier moves from $(0,0)$ to $(4,4)$ on a grid taking only unit steps east or north. A road closure blocks the junction $(2,2)$, so routes cannot pass through it. How many routes are possible?

options.why: This counts all routes, including those through the closed junction.
This is the number of routes that do pass through $(2,2)$.
Routes through $(2,2)$ number $\binom42\times\binom42$ (product of the two legs), not a sum.

hints: Count the routes that do pass through the closed junction.
A route through $(2,2)$ is a route to it followed by a route from it.
Subtract from all routes.
misconception: Adding the leg counts instead of multiplying.
why: Legs of a route through a given point are chosen independently.

sub: at most one of two groups
stem: A hiring panel of 3 is to be chosen from 6 internal and 4 external members. How many panels contain more internal than external members?

options.why: Panels with 3 internal members also have more internal than external.
This counts panels with at least one external member, including those with majority external.
The case of 1 internal and 2 external has fewer internal than external and must be excluded.

solution: More internal than external in a panel of 3 means 3 internal, or 2 internal and 1 external.
hints: Which compositions of a 3-person panel have an internal majority?
Count each composition separately.
Add the counts.
misconception: Including the minority-internal case.
why: Compositions are mutually exclusive cases.

sub: probability from counting: birthdays in a month
stem: Four colleagues each independently have a birthday in one of 12 equally likely months. What is the probability that all four birthdays are in different months? (Give a decimal to 4 places.)
hints: How many equally likely sequences of four months are there?
Count sequences with no repeated month by choosing in order.
Divide the favourable count by the total number of sequences.
misconception: Dividing by $\binom{12}{4}$ instead of $12^4$.
why: Ordered sequences are equally likely under independence.

stem: Six firms are ranked from 1 (best) to 6 (worst). In how many rankings does firm $F$ occupy a top-two position?

options.why: Firm $F$ can take either of the two top positions.
This treats the firm as equally likely to be in the top half (three positions); the condition is the top two positions.
After placing $F$ in one of two positions there are $5!$ orders for the others, not $6!$.

solution: $F$ takes position 1 or 2: 2 choices. The other 5 firms fill the remaining positions in $5! = 120$ ways.
hints: Place the special firm first: how many allowed positions?
Then arrange the other firms.
Multiply the number of allowed positions by the arrangements of the rest.
misconception: Not multiplying by the number of allowed positions.
why: Allowed positions and arrangements of the rest are independent stages.
